candidates.title: Hisense U6SF Pro Brings MiniLED Picture and Built-In Bass to Movie Night
candidates.full_text:
A movie night can start with an argument over what to watch, but the equipment shouldn’t become another topic of discussion. Hisense’s U6SF Pro brings a MiniLED screen, streaming, and a built-in subwoofer into one television, giving those pieces a shared home. Its appeal lies in how those choices accommodate an ordinary evening, from finding a film to watching the opening scene.

That evening usually begins with someone remembering an actor’s name but forgetting the movie’s title. Amazon Fire TV handles the streaming side, while the Alexa Voice Remote offers an alternative to typing with directional buttons. Pressing its voice button lets you search aloud, leaving the remote’s controls available when you want them. It won’t settle everyone’s taste, but spelling isn’t another hurdle.

Once the opening scene starts, the screen’s backlight becomes the interesting bit of design. The U6SF Pro pairs MiniLED lighting with Full Array Local Dimming, allowing different regions to adjust their illumination. Think of a light against a dark street: the goal is to give that highlight brightness without lighting the surrounding darkness equally. That’s the reason behind dividing the backlight into zones.

Hisense pairs that backlight with Hi-QLED color, which it describes as delivering vivid, lifelike colors across different kinds of content. HDR support includes Dolby Vision IQ and HDR10+ Adaptive, so the television can work with different formats rather than depending on one. The distinction matters when a film and a series arrive through different services, although the presentation still depends on what each source provides.

Of course, having picture processing doesn’t mean every movie needs more of it. Filmmaker Mode takes a more restrained approach, with settings intended to preserve aspects of the original presentation, including frame rate, aspect ratio, and color. That gives the movie’s intended presentation a place alongside the television’s enhancement features. The design decision is about knowing which adjustments to leave alone, rather than piling on effects.

An older favorite might call for a different approach when its source resolution falls short of the 4K panel. Hisense’s Hi-View AI Engine and AI 4K Upscaler are intended to refine that material for the screen. They don’t magically transform an old transfer into a modern master, but their purpose is to adapt lower-resolution material for the screen. Different content doesn’t always need identical treatment.

The soundtrack brings another piece of hardware into the story, except this one is inside the television. A built-in subwoofer forms part of the U6SF Pro’s 2.1-channel speaker system, integrating a bass driver without a separate enclosure beside the cabinet. Dolby Atmos support is included, too. It’s definitely a space saver, especially when you barely have enough room left for a dedicated sound system.

On another evening, the same screen might be connected to a gaming PC. Its native 144Hz refresh rate and two HDMI 2.1 inputs supporting up to 4K at 144Hz provide room for compatible hardware, with AMD FreeSync also included among its gaming features. Although reaching that maximum requires suitable gaming equipment and settings, at least you won’t need a different display as well.

Movie night doesn’t always come with a perfectly dark room. Someone might keep a reading lamp on, which is where the anti-reflection treatment has a practical role in reducing distracting reflections. The narrow frame follows a similar idea visually, giving the picture more prominence than its border. Neither choice asks the living room to become a dedicated theater before anyone can enjoy a film.

When the credits roll, there’s still the familiar temptation to put something else on. Perhaps that’s an old comedy with a less polished transfer, rather than another carefully graded film. The feature set accommodates both an emphasis on the original presentation and processing intended to improve lower-resolution material. You can care about a director’s intended presentation and still want some help with a favorite that predates your 4K screen.

candidates.title: Gadgeteer Daily Wrap: Sony earbuds at a record low, a $299.99 Atmos system with real rears and a Filson at half price
candidates.full_text:
Tuesday was a Black Friday pricing day on the grid, and tonight’s wrap keeps to the products, the prices and the savings. Six stops, every one published today, every price taken from its own piece.

Sony’s WF-1000XM6 earbuds are $248 on Amazon, down from $329.99, a saving of $81.99 or 25% off. Price trackers put that at the lowest Amazon price recorded for the model.

At that price the premium over rival earbuds on the same shelf shrinks, and the noise cancelling that was the reason to buy them in the first place now costs less to get.

The Hisense AX5140Q is a 5.1.4-channel soundbar system with a wireless subwoofer and wireless rear speakers in the box, cut to $299.99 from $399.99 for Black Friday, a $100 saving.

Most soundbar deals stop at the bar and the subwoofer. This one puts speakers behind the couch at the same $299.99, on Amazon and at Hisense.

Filson’s Spokane Insulated Cruiser Jacket adds insulation to the 1914 Cruiser pattern, and the Red/Black Windowpane colorway runs $224.50 against a $449 list price, exactly 50% off.

Sizes XS, S, M and XL were still on the rack when the piece published, while L, 2XL and 3XL were gone.

The Oura Ring 5 in Gold, size 7, is $394.20 at Amazon against a $499 list price, a 21% cut on the finish that usually carries the premium.

The Ring 5 shrank the hardware 40% against the Ring 4 while keeping the full tracking stack, in titanium with recessed sensors.

Brooks’ Adrenaline GTS 25, the men’s stability trainer now in its 25th generation, costs $109.95 on Amazon, down 29% from its $155 list price, a $45.05 saving.

Prices start at $109.95 and climb with size and color, and the shoe holds a 4.5-star rating from 3,164 ratings on Amazon.

The Harman Kardon SoundSticks 4, the transparent dome subwoofer and satellite pair people remember from the clear iMac era, are $149.99 in Harman Kardon’s own store, half of the $299.95 list price.

Amazon’s cut on the same white system is smaller at $199.95, still $100 under list.

candidates.title: Genspark built a five-button remote for your AI agents, and it has Cherry mechanical switches
candidates.full_text:
The QWERTY layout turned 150 a couple of years ago, and we’re still hammering out AI prompts on a design built for 1870s typewriters. Meanwhile, the average person types around 40 words a minute and speaks closer to 160. Genspark, the Palo Alto company behind Genspark AI Workspace, is betting on that gap with the SecondBrain VoicePad, a palm-sized aluminum gadget with five keys and two microphones. Press a key, say what you want, and the words appear wherever your cursor is blinking. Your keyboard keeps its job, though it now has a very chatty coworker.

VoicePad weighs 85 grams (about 3 ounces) and has a CNC-machined aluminum body. Out of the box, its keys handle dictation, meeting notes, your calendar, slide decks, and Genspark’s AI agent. Each can be remapped to open ChatGPT, Claude, Slack, or whatever app runs your day. It connects to a Mac or PC over Bluetooth or USB-C and records meetings on its own when your laptop is nowhere nearby.

Genspark describes VoicePad as “designed like jewelry, built like a tool.” Four square keys and one wide bar sit inside a single aluminum frame, rising just above the metal so they’re easier to find by touch. A dense grid of perforations across the top hides the speaker and microphones, giving it a pocket-radio look that Dieter Rams fans will clock immediately. A tiny slide switch handles power on the side, with a status light beside it, and USB-C sits on the bottom edge. A magnetic mount and an included metal plate let it park wherever you stick that plate.

Under those keys sit Cherry MX Ultra Low Profile tactile switches, a nerdy choice for a five-button gadget. Cherry launched the ULP in 2021 as its flattest mechanical switch, roughly 0.14 inches (3.5mm) tall and built for ultra-thin laptop keyboards. Total travel is 0.07 inches (1.8mm), with a tactile bump at 0.8mm rather than a deliberate click. Cherry rates them for more than 50 million keystrokes. I like that Genspark picked a mechanical switch here, because a push-to-talk key you hit hundreds of times a day should feel crisp rather than mushy.

Hold the wide bottom key, talk, let go, and your words land at the cursor, from email and Slack to documents and your terminal. Genspark says voice typing works in more than 100 apps, stripping out filler words and false starts so a rambling “so, uh, basically” becomes a cleaner sentence. It also says the software handles details that can trip up dictation, such as formatting “forty eight thousand two fifty” as $48,250 or spelling Siobhán with the accent. The comparison between speaking at roughly 160 words a minute and typing at 40 is the basis for Genspark’s “up to 4x faster” claim, rather than a guarantee of finished writing speed.

Whisper support is the detail I find most appealing. Talking to your computer in an open office is socially terrifying, because everyone hears you ask ChatGPT to “make this email sound less passive-aggressive,” and suddenly the whole floor knows who it’s about. Genspark says VoicePad’s dual microphones can pick up whispered dictation when you hold it close to your mouth. That could make it more practical in shared apartments or on late-night couches where someone’s asleep in the next room. Voice input has a social problem as much as a technical one, and a mic you can hold close is a simple way to address it.

The default layout covers Meeting Notes, Calendar, Slides, AI Workspace, and Dictate, and none of it is locked in. Open the Genspark Super App on your Mac or PC, pick a key, and give it a new job, triggered by a tap or a hold. Keys can launch ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Notion, or any installed app, or use shortcuts such as Copy, Paste, and Enter. Genspark even suggests starter layouts, giving writers Rewrite, Polish, and Memo, while developers get Terminal Helper, Claude, and ChatGPT. For voice input, the basic flow stays the same: tap a key to open the app, hold the wide bar, and talk.

Translation is the feature I expect to win over the most people. Set a key to Translate, hold it, and speak in any of more than 50 supported languages, including Japanese, Korean, Chinese, Spanish, French, German, and Portuguese. Let go, and the software inserts an English translation into the chat or document you have open.
